newsitem.title: USA: U.S. House panel advised on housing tax credits.
newsitem.headline: U.S. House panel advised on housing tax credits.

text.p: A parade of state and local housing groups on Thursday offered a key U.S. House panel a raft of ideas on how to improve the Low Income Housing Tax Credit program.

Representatiaves from Texas, California, Maryland, Connecticut and other parts of the country testified at the second day of hearings on the issue by the House Ways and Means Committee's subpanel on oversight, chaired by Rep. Nancy Johnson, R-Conn.
The hearings follow General Accounting Office findings earlier this month that the tax credit program generally works but needs some improvement.
Ways and Means Committee Chairman Bill Archer, R-Texas, who sought to sunset the program in 1995, said after reading GAO's report that the program appears to be well targeted.
He stressed, however, that compliance with and enforcement of the program need to be strengthened and asked his panel's oversight subcommittee to hold hearings on the issue.
The municipal bond market is interested in the program because the housing credit often is used in conjunction with tax-exempt housing bonds.

Johnson, chair of the oversight panel, said in opening Thursday's hearing: "The credit has helped finance the construction and rehabilitation of a significant amount of housing for low-income Americans."
"But ... there are several opportunities to improve the administration of the credit. I am looking forward to suggestions."

U.S. Rep. Jack Metcalf, R-Wash., chairman of the Republican Housing Opportunity Caucus, said his top recommendation is that Congress assure housing investors that the tax credit will remain a permanent federal program.
"Returning to the stop-start status to which the Tax Credit was subjected before 1993 will disrupt the program just when it is reaching peak efficiency," Metcalf said.
Metcalf also recommended that Congress see that small developers have more access to tax credits and that it require developers to present market feasibility studies before construction begins.
Herbert Stevens, a partner with Peabody & Brown, which specializes in the tax credit program, said states should develop better guidelines on how to produce quality housing.
"Congress and the states should be careful to avoid the 'cheaper is better' assumption," he said.

William Haynsworth, president of the Affordable Housing Tax Credit Coalition, took issue with charges made at the panel's first oversight hearing on the program last week that the tax credit costs the federal government more than Section 8 housing certificates.

"That comparison is simply not fair or apt," Haynsworth said. "Unlike the tax credit, a (Section 8) voucher does not build or rehabilitate housing, it simply provides rental assistance if the recipient is fortunate enought to find suitable housing," he said.
Also, HUD says that a significant number of certificates are returned unused because of a shortage of affordable housing, he said.
